docs.title: Key Points of Encapsulation
docs.text:
• Wrap data and methods in a class.
  • Hide fields using access modifiers (private, default, protected, public).
  • Provide controlled access using getters/setters.
  • Static variables can also be encapsulated (class-level data).
  • Validation logic can be added in setters.

docs.title: Access Modifiers in Encapsulation
docs.text: Modifier Access Level Encapsulation Use Case private Only within the class Most common for encapsulation default Within the same package Less common, package-level control protected Within package + subclasses (even in different package) For inheritance-based encapsulation public Anywhere Usually avoid for fields, used for methods/getters

docs.title: Complex Encapsulation Example
docs.text:
package com.example.encapsulation;

// Employee class demonstrating encapsulation
public class Employee {

    // Private instance variables (best practice)
    private String name;
    private int age;

    // Protected variable (accessible in subclasses)
    protected String department;

    // Default access variable (accessible in same package)
    String project;

    // Public variable (less recommended)
    public String company;

    // Static variable (class-level, shared across objects)
    private static int employeeCount = 0;

    // Constructor
    public Employee(String name, int age, String department, String project, String company) {
        setName(name);       // Using setter for validation
        setAge(age);         // Using setter for validation
        this.department = department;
        this.project = project;
        this.company = company;

        employeeCount++;     // Increment static count
    }

    // ----------------------
    // Getters & Setters
    // ----------------------

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        if(name == null || name.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.println("Invalid name!");
        } else {
            this.name = name;
        }
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        if(age < 18 || age > 65) {
            System.out.println("Age must be between 18 and 65");
        } else {
            this.age = age;
        }
    }

    // Getter for static variable
    public static int getEmployeeCount() {
        return employeeCount;
    }

    // No setter for employeeCount (read-only) to protect encapsulation

    // Method to display info
    public void displayInfo() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println("Department: " + department);
        System.out.println("Project: " + project);
        System.out.println("Company: " + company);
        System.out.println("Total Employees: " + employeeCount);
    }
}

docs.title: Main Class Example
docs.text:
package com.example.encapsulation;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Create employee objects
        Employee emp1 = new Employee("Alice", 25, "IT", "Automation", "TechCorp");
        Employee emp2 = new Employee("Bob", 30, "HR", "Recruitment", "TechCorp");

        // Accessing fields through getters and setters
        System.out.println("Employee 1 Name: " + emp1.getName());
        emp1.setAge(17);  // Invalid age, setter validation triggers
        emp1.setAge(28);  // Valid

        // Accessing protected, default, and public variables directly
        System.out.println("Employee 1 Department: " + emp1.department); // Protected
        System.out.println("Employee 1 Project: " + emp1.project);       // Default
        System.out.println("Employee 1 Company: " + emp1.company);       // Public

        // Display info
        emp1.displayInfo();
        emp2.displayInfo();

        // Access static variable
        System.out.println("Total employees: " + Employee.getEmployeeCount());
    }
}

docs.title: Private Variables + Getter/Setter
docs.text:
• Encapsulated name and age with validation in setter.
  • Prevents illegal data entry (core principle of encapsulation).

docs.title: Static Variable
docs.text:
• employeeCount is class-level.
  • Getter allows controlled read access; no setter keeps it read-only.

docs.title: Access Modifiers
docs.text:
• private → fully hidden.
  • protected → accessible in subclass (good for inheritance scenarios).
  • default → accessible in same package (package-level encapsulation).
  • public → accessible everywhere (should avoid for fields; use for methods instead).

docs.title: Encapsulation + OOP
docs.text:
• Combines data hiding, validation, and controlled access.
  • Prepares your code for safe inheritance and reuse.

💡 Interview Tip: A complex encapsulation question might ask:

“Can you make a static variable private and expose it via getter? Can you combine all access modifiers in one class?”

docs.title: 💌 Definition
docs.text: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of OOP. It means binding data (fields) and methods (functions) together into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access to the data by making fields private and providing controlled access via public methods (getters/setters).

docs.title: 🔑 Why Encapsulation?
docs.text:
If fields are public:

  • Anyone can directly access or modify them.
  • No control over invalid data.
  • Difficult to maintain or change internal representation later.

With encapsulation:

  • Data is hidden from outside classes.
  • Access is controlled through methods.
  • Validation and business rules can be applied.

docs.title: ✅ Key Features
docs.text:
1. Private fields → data hiding.
  2. Public getters/setters → controlled access.
  3. Validation → prevent invalid values.
  4. Read-only / Write-only → allow only getter or only setter.
  5. Flexibility → change implementation without breaking outside code.

docs.title: 📝 Example Without Encapsulation (Problem)
docs.text:
class Student {
    public int age;   // public field
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.age = -10;   // ❌ invalid, but allowed
        System.out.println("Age: " + s.age);
    }
}

docs.title: 📝 Example With Encapsulation (Solution)
docs.text:
class Student {
    private int age;  // private field

    // Setter with validation
    public void setAge(int age) {
        if(age > 0) {
            this.age = age;
        } else {
            System.out.println("❌ Age must be positive!");
        }
    }

    // Getter
    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s = new Student();
        s.setAge(-10); // blocked
        s.setAge(20);  // ✅ valid
        System.out.println("Age: " + s.getAge());
    }
}

docs.title: 🌟 Real-World Example: Bank Account
docs.text:
class BankAccount {
    private double balance; // sensitive data

    public BankAccount(double initialBalance) {
        if(initialBalance >= 0) {
            this.balance = initialBalance;
        }
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance; // read-only access
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if(amount > 0) balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if(amount > 0 && amount <= balance) balance -= amount;
        else System.out.println("❌ Invalid transaction");
    }
}

public class BankDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount acc = new BankAccount(1000);
        acc.deposit(500);
        acc.withdraw(2000); // ❌ not allowed
        System.out.println("Final Balance: " + acc.getBalance());
    }
}

docs.title: ⭐ Advantages of Encapsulation
docs.text:
• Protects data integrity.
  • Improves code maintainability.
  • Provides flexibility to change internal implementation.
  • Enhances security by exposing only necessary details.
  • Supports abstraction (hiding unnecessary details).

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text:
Encapsulation = Data Hiding + Controlled Access

  • Keep fields private.
  • Use getter and setter methods.
  • Apply validation logic inside setters.
  • Make class fields read-only/write-only when required.

docs.title: 🔹 Encapsulation in Selenium Java Framework
docs.text: In Selenium frameworks, Encapsulation is heavily used in Page Object Model (POM):

docs.title: Example: Page Object
docs.text:
import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver;
import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.FindBy;
import org.openqa.selenium.support.PageFactory;

public class LoginPage {
    private WebDriver driver;  // private driver reference

    // Private WebElements
    @FindBy(id = "username")
    private WebElement usernameField;

    @FindBy(id = "password")
    private WebElement passwordField;

    @FindBy(id = "loginBtn")
    private WebElement loginButton;

    // Constructor
    public LoginPage(WebDriver driver) {
        this.driver = driver;
        PageFactory.initElements(driver, this);
    }

    // Public methods (encapsulation) to interact with elements
    public void enterUsername(String username) {
        usernameField.sendKeys(username);
    }

    public void enterPassword(String password) {
        passwordField.sendKeys(password);
    }

    public void clickLogin() {
        loginButton.click();
    }
}

Explanation:

  • Fields (WebElement) are private → hidden from test classes.
  • Test classes access elements only via public methods → controlled interaction.
  • Improves maintainability: If locators change, only the Page class changes.

docs.title: 🔹 Encapsulation in Java Playwright Framework
docs.text: Similarly, in Playwright (Java) framework, encapsulation is used for page objects:

docs.title: Example: Login Page
docs.text:
import com.microsoft.playwright.Page;

public class LoginPage {
    private Page page;  // private Playwright page object

    // Private locators
    private final String usernameInput = "#username";
    private final String passwordInput = "#password";
    private final String loginBtn = "#loginBtn";

    // Constructor
    public LoginPage(Page page) {
        this.page = page;
    }

    // Public methods to interact with page
    public void enterUsername(String username) {
        page.locator(usernameInput).fill(username);
    }

    public void enterPassword(String password) {
        page.locator(passwordInput).fill(password);
    }

    public void clickLogin() {
        page.locator(loginBtn).click();
    }
}

Explanation:

  • Locators are private → hidden from test scripts.
  • Test scripts call public methods → controlled access.
  • If locators change, only LoginPage needs update.

docs.title: ✅ Conclusion
docs.text:
Encapsulation in Java is not just a theory, it is widely applied in automation frameworks:

  • Protects element locators and driver/page objects.
  • Provides controlled methods to interact with UI.
  • Improves maintainability, readability, and security of your automation code.

docs.title: Advanced Inheritance in Java with Static Methods and Constructors
Key Points
docs.text:
• Subclasses inherit properties and methods from a superclass.
  • Static variables/methods belong to the class and can be shared across instances.
  • Constructors initialize objects; subclasses can call superclass constructors using super().
  • Method overriding demonstrates runtime polymorphism.
  • Access modifiers control visibility (private, protected, public).

docs.title: Complex Inheritance Example
docs.text:
package com.example.inheritance;

// Superclass
class Employee {
    protected String name;
    private int age;
    public String company;
    protected static int employeeCount = 0;

    // User-defined constructor
    public Employee(String name, int age, String company) {
        this.name = name;
        setAge(age);  // Encapsulation in action
        this.company = company;
        employeeCount++;
        System.out.println("Employee constructor called for " + name);
    }

    // Getter and Setter for private field
    public void setAge(int age) {
        if(age < 18 || age > 65) {
            System.out.println("Age must be between 18 and 65");
        } else {
            this.age = age;
        }
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    // Instance method
    public void displayInfo() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Age: " + age);
        System.out.println("Company: " + company);
    }

    // Static method
    public static void showEmployeeCount() {
        System.out.println("Total Employees: " + employeeCount);
    }
}

// Subclass
class Manager extends Employee {
    private String department;

    // Subclass constructor
    public Manager(String name, int age, String company, String department) {
        super(name, age, company); // Call superclass constructor
        this.department = department;
        System.out.println("Manager constructor called for " + name);
    }

    // Method overriding
    @Override
    public void displayInfo() {
        super.displayInfo(); // Call superclass method
        System.out.println("Department: " + department);
    }

    // Subclass-specific method
    public void approveLeave() {
        System.out.println(name + " approved leave for the team.");
    }

    // Static method in subclass (hides superclass static method)
    public static void showEmployeeCount() {
        System.out.println("Manager count: " + employeeCount);
    }
}

docs.title: Testing Inheritance with Static Methods and Constructors
docs.text:
package com.example.inheritance;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Create Employee and Manager objects
        Employee emp1 = new Employee("Alice", 28, "TechCorp");
        Manager mgr1 = new Manager("Bob", 35, "TechCorp", "IT");

        System.out.println("\n--- Display Info ---");
        emp1.displayInfo();
        mgr1.displayInfo(); // Overridden method

        System.out.println("\n--- Approve Leave ---");
        mgr1.approveLeave();

        System.out.println("\n--- Static Methods ---");
        Employee.showEmployeeCount(); // Calls superclass static method
        Manager.showEmployeeCount();  // Calls subclass static method (hides superclass)

        // Access modifiers demonstration
        System.out.println("\n--- Access Modifiers ---");
        System.out.println("Manager Name (protected): " + mgr1.name);
        System.out.println("Manager Company (public): " + mgr1.company);
        // System.out.println(mgr1.age); // ❌ private, cannot access directly
    }
}

docs.title: User-defined Constructors
docs.text:
• Superclass and subclass constructors are called in order of inheritance.
  • super() ensures proper initialization of superclass fields.

docs.title: Static Variables and Methods
docs.text:
• employeeCount is shared across all instances.
  • Static methods in subclasses hide superclass static methods, not override.

docs.title: Method Overriding
docs.text:
• Subclass displayInfo() overrides superclass method for custom behavior.
  • super.displayInfo() can still be called inside overridden method.

docs.title: Access Modifiers
docs.text:
• private → fully hidden, accessed via getter/setter.
  • protected → accessible in subclass.
  • public → accessible everywhere.

docs.title: Encapsulation + Inheritance
docs.text:
• Private members remain encapsulated, even in subclasses.
  • Protected/public members allow safe inheritance and reuse.

docs.title: 📌 Definition
docs.text:
Inheritance is an OOP concept where one class (child/subclass) inherits properties and methods from another class (parent/superclass). It allows code reuse and hierarchical class structure.

Syntax:

class Parent {
    // parent class code
}

class Child extends Parent {
    // child class code
}

docs.title: 🔑 Why Inheritance?
docs.text:
• Reusability: Write common code in parent, reuse in child.
  • Maintainability: Changes in parent reflect in child classes.
  • Polymorphism: Parent reference can refer to child object.
  • Hierarchical structure: Model real-world relationships.

docs.title: ✅ Types of Inheritance in Java
docs.text:
1. Single Inheritance: One child, one parent
  2. Multilevel Inheritance: A → B → C
  3. Hierarchical Inheritance: One parent, multiple children

Note: Java does not support multiple inheritance with classes (can use interfaces for that).

docs.title: 📝 Basic Example: Single Inheritance
docs.text:
// Parent class
class Animal {
    void eat() {
        System.out.println("This animal eats food.");
    }
}

// Child class
class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks.");
    }
}

public class InheritanceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog d = new Dog();
        d.eat();  // inherited method
        d.bark(); // child’s own method
    }
}

docs.title: 📝 Example: Multilevel Inheritance
docs.text:
class Vehicle {
    void start() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle starts");
    }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    void honk() {
        System.out.println("Car honks");
    }
}

class SportsCar extends Car {
    void turbo() {
        System.out.println("SportsCar turbo mode");
    }
}

public class MultilevelDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SportsCar sc = new SportsCar();
        sc.start(); // from Vehicle
        sc.honk();  // from Car
        sc.turbo(); // from SportsCar
    }
}

docs.title: 📝 Example: Hierarchical Inheritance
docs.text:
class Vehicle {
    void start() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle starts");
    }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    void honk() {
        System.out.println("Car honks");
    }
}

class Bike extends Vehicle {
    void ringBell() {
        System.out.println("Bike rings bell");
    }
}

public class HierarchicalDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Car car = new Car();
        car.start();
        car.honk();

        Bike bike = new Bike();
        bike.start();
        bike.ringBell();
    }
}

docs.title: 🔹 Real-World Example in Selenium Java Framework
docs.text:
In Page Object Model, inheritance is used for BasePage:

import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver;

public class BasePage {
    protected WebDriver driver;

    public BasePage(WebDriver driver) {
        this.driver = driver;
    }

    public void openUrl(String url) {
        driver.get(url);
    }
}

// Child Page inherits BasePage
public class LoginPage extends BasePage {
    public LoginPage(WebDriver driver) {
        super(driver); // call parent constructor
    }

    public void login(String user, String pass) {
        // code to perform login
    }
}

Explanation:

  • Common methods like openUrl() are in BasePage → reused in all pages.
  • Child pages inherit these methods → avoids duplicate code.

docs.title: 🔹 Real-World Example in Java Playwright Framework
docs.text:
import com.microsoft.playwright.Page;

// Base class
public class BasePage {
    protected Page page;

    public BasePage(Page page) {
        this.page = page;
    }

    public void navigateTo(String url) {
        page.navigate(url);
    }
}

// Child Page
public class LoginPage extends BasePage {
    private final String usernameInput = "#username";
    private final String passwordInput = "#password";
    private final String loginBtn = "#loginBtn";

    public LoginPage(Page page) {
        super(page);
    }

    public void login(String user, String pass) {
        page.locator(usernameInput).fill(user);
        page.locator(passwordInput).fill(pass);
        page.locator(loginBtn).click();
    }
}

Explanation:

  • BasePage contains common page methods (like navigateTo()).
  • LoginPage inherits them → can reuse in all other page objects.

docs.title: ⭐ Advantages of Inheritance
docs.text:
1. Code reusability → avoids duplication.
  2. Logical structure → parent-child relationship.
  3. Easy maintenance → modify in parent, affects all children.
  4. Supports polymorphism (child object can be referenced by parent type).

docs.title: Java Control Statements for Software Testers
docs.text: This chapter explains decision-making and looping constructs in Java with real testing examples, retry logic, and interview questions with code.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Executes a block of code only when a condition is true.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
if (condition) {
    // code
}

docs.title: Tester Example – Validate Login Result
docs.text:
boolean isLoggedIn = true;

if (isLoggedIn) {
    System.out.println("Login Test Passed");
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: When should you use if instead of if-else? A: When you only want to act on a true condition and do nothing otherwise.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Provides an alternative path when the condition is false.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
if (condition) {
    // true block
} else {
    // false block
}

docs.title: Tester Example – API Status Validation
docs.text:
int statusCode = 401;

if (statusCode == 200) {
    System.out.println("API Test Passed");
} else {
    System.out.println("API Test Failed");
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Can else exist without if? A: No. else must always be associated with an if.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Used to check multiple conditions sequentially.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
if (condition1) {
} else if (condition2) {
} else {
}

docs.title: Tester Example – Response Validation
docs.text:
int statusCode = 404;

if (statusCode == 200) {
    System.out.println("Success");
} else if (statusCode == 401) {
    System.out.println("Unauthorized");
} else if (statusCode == 404) {
    System.out.println("Not Found");
} else {
    System.out.println("Unexpected Response");
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: How many else-if blocks are allowed? A: Unlimited, but only one block executes.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Cleaner alternative to multiple else-if when comparing fixed values.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
switch (expression) {
    case value:
        break;
    default:
}

docs.title: Tester Example – Browser Selection
docs.text:
String browser = "chrome";

switch (browser) {
    case "chrome":
        System.out.println("Launching Chrome");
        break;
    case "firefox":
        System.out.println("Launching Firefox");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Unsupported Browser");
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Why is break important in switch? A: Without break, execution continues to the next case (fall-through).

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Used when the number of iterations is known.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
for (initialization; condition; increment) {
}

docs.title: Tester Example – Loop Through Test Data
docs.text:
String[] users = {"admin", "guest", "tester"};

for (int i = 0; i < users.length; i++) {
    System.out.println("Testing login for: " + users[i]);
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: When is for preferred over while? A: When iteration count is fixed or predictable.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Executes while a condition remains true. Condition is checked before execution.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
while (condition) {
}

docs.title: Tester Example – Wait for Element
docs.text:
int attempts = 0;

while (attempts < 3) {
    System.out.println("Checking element...");
    attempts++;
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: What is the risk with while loops? A: Infinite loops if the condition never becomes false.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Executes at least once, condition checked after execution.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
do {
} while (condition);

docs.title: Tester Example – Retry Logic
docs.text:
int retry = 1;

do {
    System.out.println("Retry attempt: " + retry);
    retry++;
} while (retry <= 3);

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Difference between while and do-while? A: do-while runs at least once even if condition is false.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Terminates loop or switch immediately.

docs.title: Tester Example – Stop on Failure
docs.text:
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) {
        System.out.println("Critical failure found");
        break;
    }
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Can break be used outside loops? A: No, only inside loops or switch.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text: Skips current iteration and moves to the next one.

docs.title: Tester Example – Skip Disabled Test Case
docs.text:
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 2) {
        continue;
    }
    System.out.println("Executing test case: " + i);
}

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text: Q: Difference between break and continue? A: break exits loop; continue skips iteration.

docs.title: 🧪 Testing Use-Case Summary
docs.text: Scenario Java Construct Login validation if / if-else Browser selection switch Data-driven tests for loop Wait & polling while Retry mechanism do-while Stop execution break Skip test continue

docs.title: ✅ Interview Tip
docs.text: Control statements form the backbone of test automation logic. If you master these, frameworks become easy.

docs.title: 📌 Definition
docs.text:
Polymorphism is an OOP concept that means “one name, many forms”. It allows a single method, object, or operator to behave differently based on context.

Types:

  1. Compile-Time (Method Overloading)
  2. Run-Time (Method Overriding)

docs.title: 🔑 Why Polymorphism?
docs.text:
• Improves code readability.
  • Reduces complexity by using the same method name for different tasks.
  • Supports flexibility in code design.
  • Helps in maintainable and reusable code.

docs.title: 1. Compile-Time Polymorphism (Method Overloading)
docs.text:
• Same method name but different parameter types or number.
  • Resolved by compiler.

Example:

class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

public class OverloadingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator calc = new Calculator();
        System.out.println(calc.add(5, 3));       // int version
        System.out.println(calc.add(2.5, 3.5));   // double version
        System.out.println(calc.add(1, 2, 3));    // 3 params
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Run-Time Polymorphism (Method Overriding)
docs.text:
• Child class overrides parent method with same name & signature.
  • Decided by JVM at runtime which method to call.

Example:

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound.");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks.");
    }
}

public class OverridingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal obj = new Dog();  // Parent reference, child object
        obj.sound();             // Runtime decides -> Dog barks.
    }
}

docs.title: 🔹 Complex Example: Polymorphism in Banking
docs.text:
abstract class Account {
    abstract void calculateInterest();
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Savings Account interest: 4%");
    }
}

class FixedDepositAccount extends Account {
    @Override
    void calculateInterest() {
        System.out.println("Fixed Deposit interest: 6%");
    }
}

public class BankDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Account acc1 = new SavingsAccount();
        Account acc2 = new FixedDepositAccount();

        acc1.calculateInterest();  // Savings Account interest: 4%
        acc2.calculateInterest();  // Fixed Deposit interest: 6%
    }
}

Explanation: Same method calculateInterest() behaves differently → runtime polymorphism.

docs.title: 🔹 Polymorphism in Selenium Java Framework
docs.text:
import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver;

public class BasePage {
    protected WebDriver driver;

    public BasePage(WebDriver driver) {
        this.driver = driver;
    }

    // Overloaded method example
    public void openUrl(String url) {
        driver.get(url);
    }

    public void openUrl(String url, boolean maximize) {
        driver.get(url);
        if(maximize) driver.manage().window().maximize();
    }
}

Explanation:

  • openUrl() is overloaded → compile-time polymorphism.
  • All pages inherit BasePage → runtime polymorphism when child overrides methods.

docs.title: 🔹 Polymorphism in Java Playwright Framework
docs.text:
import com.microsoft.playwright.Page;

public class BasePage {
    protected Page page;

    public BasePage(Page page) {
        this.page = page;
    }

    // Compile-time polymorphism
    public void navigate(String url) {
        page.navigate(url);
    }

    public void navigate(String url, int timeout) {
        page.navigate(url, new Page.NavigateOptions().setTimeout(timeout));
    }
}

public class LoginPage extends BasePage {
    public LoginPage(Page page) {
        super(page);
    }

    // Runtime polymorphism
    @Override
    public void navigate(String url) {
        System.out.println("LoginPage custom navigate");
        super.navigate(url);
    }
}

Explanation:

  • Overloaded navigate() → compile-time polymorphism.
  • Overridden navigate() → runtime polymorphism.

docs.title: ⭐ Advantages of Polymorphism
docs.text:
1. Improves code readability.
  2. Promotes reusability.
  3. Reduces complex code with common methods.
  4. Supports flexible and maintainable automation frameworks.

docs.title: ArrayList – In‑Depth Interview Notes
docs.text: This document explains ArrayList as a data structure, covering internal working, performance, shifting behavior, and when to use it, at an interview‑ready level.

docs.title: 1. What is ArrayList?
docs.text:
ArrayList is a resizable (dynamic) array implementation of the List interface.

  • Stores elements in contiguous memory
  • Backed internally by an Object[] array
  • Allows duplicate elements
  • Maintains insertion order
  • Provides index‑based access

docs.title: 2. Internal Structure
docs.text:
Internally, ArrayList looks like this:

public class ArrayList<E> {
    transient Object[] elementData; // internal array
    private int size;               // number of elements
}
  • elementData stores references to objects, not actual objects
  • Each slot holds a reference (4 or 8 bytes depending on JVM)

docs.title: Logical View
docs.text:
Index:   0     1     2     3
Array:  A     B     C     D

docs.title: 3. Capacity vs Size
docs.text:
• Size → Number of elements actually stored
  • Capacity → Length of internal array
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
  • Initial capacity = 10 (created lazily)
  • Size starts from 0

docs.title: 4. How ArrayList Grows (Resizing)
docs.text:
When the internal array becomes full:

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1); // 1.5x growth

docs.title: What happens during resize?
docs.text:
1. New larger array is created
  2. Old elements are copied using System.arraycopy()
  3. Old array becomes eligible for GC

⛔ Resize is costly because it copies all existing references

docs.title: Example
docs.text: list.add(1, "X");

docs.title: Before insertion
docs.text:
Index:  0   1   2   3
        A   B   C   D

docs.title: After insertion
docs.text:
Index:  0   1   2   3   4
        A   X   B   C   D

docs.title: What actually shifts?
docs.text:
⚠️ Not raw memory bytes

✔ Java shifts object references inside the Object[]

docs.title: Internal operation
docs.text:
System.arraycopy(
    elementData,   // source
    index,         // start position
    elementData,   // destination
    index + 1,     // shift right
    size - index   // number of references
);

📌 This is an O(n) operation

docs.title: Example
docs.text: list.remove(1);

docs.title: Before removal
docs.text: A   B   C   D

docs.title: After removal
docs.text: A   C   D

docs.title: Internal behavior
docs.text:
System.arraycopy(
    elementData,
    index + 1,
    elementData,
    index,
    size - index - 1
);

elementData[--size] = null; // avoid memory leak

✔ Last reference is set to null to help Garbage Collection

docs.title: Cost factors
docs.text:
• Multiple reference moves
  • CPU cache invalidation
  • Larger array → more shifting
  • Frequent insert/remove → high CPU usage

docs.title: Worst case example
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    list.add(0, i); // worst case
}

📉 Time complexity becomes O(n²)

docs.title: 8. Resize + Shift = Double Cost
docs.text:
Worst scenario during insertion:

  1. Array is full → resize (copy all elements)
  2. Insert at index → shift elements again

📌 Two expensive operations in one call

docs.title: 9. Time Complexity Summary
docs.text: Operation Complexity Reason get(index) O(1) Direct index access add(e) O(1)* Amortized add(index, e) O(n) Shifting remove(index) O(n) Shifting contains() O(n) Linear search

docs.text:
After add operations: [Java, Go, Python]

get(0): Java
After set(1, Rust): [Java, Rust, Python]
After remove(0): [Rust, Python]

contains(Java): false
size(): 2
isEmpty(): false

After addAll(): [Rust, Python, C++, JavaScript]
After addAll(index, list): [Rust, C++, JavaScript, Python, C++, JavaScript]
After manual loop add: [Rust, C++, JavaScript, Python, C++, JavaScript, C++, JavaScript]

After clear(): []
After new ArrayList<>(): [NewItem]
After removeAll(): []

docs.title: 11. System.arraycopy() – Important Notes
docs.text:
public static native void arraycopy(...);
  • Implemented in JVM (C/C++), not Java
  • Uses optimized native memory copy
  • Much faster than manual loops
  • Still O(n)

❌ Cannot view Java source ✔ Can observe behavior via benchmarks

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Contiguous memory
  • Cache‑friendly
  • Very fast read operations

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Costly shifting
  • Resize overhead

docs.title: 13. When to Use ArrayList
docs.text:
✔ Read‑heavy operations ✔ Frequent get(index) calls ✔ Append‑only scenarios ✔ Configuration or static data

❌ Avoid when:

  • Frequent insert/delete in middle
  • Large dynamic modifications

docs.title: 14. ArrayList vs LinkedList (Quick View)
docs.text: Feature ArrayList LinkedList Internal DS Dynamic Array Doubly Linked List Memory Less More (prev/next) get(index) O(1) O(n) Insert middle O(n) (shift) O(1)* Cache friendly Yes No

docs.title: 15. Interview‑Ready Explanation (Use This)
docs.text: ArrayList internally uses a dynamic Object array. When we insert or remove an element at a specific index, the subsequent elements must be shifted using System.arraycopy. Although only object references are moved, this still causes O(n) time complexity and impacts performance for large lists with frequent modifications. However, ArrayList offers excellent read performance due to contiguous memory layout.

docs.title: 16. Key Takeaways
docs.text:
✔ Backed by Object[] ✔ Shifts references, not raw bytes ✔ Insert/remove in middle is expensive ✔ Best choice for read‑heavy use cases ✔ Default List implementation in real projects

End of Notes

HashMap<E, Object> map;
  • Elements are stored as keys

docs.title: ✅ Step 1 — hashCode() is generated
docs.text:
"ACC123".hashCode();

Example:

hashCode = 12345678

Purpose

  • Convert object → integer
  • Decide storage location

docs.title: ✅ Step 2 — Bucket index is calculated
docs.text:
HashMap has an internal bucket array.

Default size:

16 buckets

Formula:

index = hashCode % arraySize;

Example:

12345678 % 16 = 14

➡ Stored in bucket[14]

docs.title: ✅ Step 3 — Stored in bucket
docs.text:
Java checks:

👉 Is bucket[14] empty?

Case 1: Empty

bucket[14] → "ACC123"

Case 2: Collision

bucket[14] → [ACC120, ACC121]

Java adds it using collision handling.

Internally

  • Java 7 → LinkedList
  • Java 8+ → LinkedList → Tree (if many collisions)

docs.title: ✅ Step 4 — Duplicate check using equals()
docs.text:
Java compares:

existingElement.equals(newElement);

Example:

"ACC123".equals("ACC123") → true
  • ✅ true → Duplicate → NOT added
  • ❌ false → Unique → Added

⚠️ IMPORTANT RULE

HashSet uses both hashCode() and equals()

docs.title: 🔁 Summary Flow (Interview Gold)
docs.text:
add(element)
   ↓
hashCode()
   ↓
bucket index calculation
   ↓
check bucket
   ↓
equals() comparison
   ↓
add OR ignore

docs.title: ⚠️ Why BOTH hashCode() and equals() are needed?
docs.text:
Different objects may have same hashCode:

"ABC"
"CBA"

➡ Same bucket

So Java uses:

  • hashCode() → bucket
  • equals() → actual equality

docs.title: 🧪 Custom Object Example (Very Important)
docs.text:
class Account {
    String accNo;
}

If you don’t override:

equals()
hashCode()

set.add(new Account("A1"));
set.add(new Account("A1"));

❌ Duplicates allowed!

docs.title: Correct Way
docs.text:
@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return accNo.hashCode();
}

@Override
public boolean equals(Object obj) {
    Account other = (Account) obj;
    return this.accNo.equals(other.accNo);
}

txnIds.add("TXN1001");
txnIds.add("TXN1001"); // ignored automatically

  • equals() → duplicate detection

docs.title: LinkedList – From Scratch to Expert (Interview Notes)
docs.text: This document explains LinkedList in Java from beginner to expert level, covering internal working, indexing behavior, performance, memory usage, and when to use it, in an interview-ready format.

docs.title: 1. What is a LinkedList?
docs.text:
A LinkedList is a linear data structure where elements are stored as nodes.

Each node contains: - The actual data - Reference(s) to neighboring nodes

Unlike arrays or ArrayList: - Elements are not stored in contiguous memory - There is no direct random access

docs.title: 2. Why LinkedList Exists
docs.text:
Problems with arrays / ArrayList: - Costly insert/delete due to shifting - Fixed size (arrays)

LinkedList solves: - Dynamic size - Easy insertion and deletion

But introduces: - Slower access - Higher memory usage

docs.title: Singly Linked List
docs.text:
A → B → C → D → null

graphql Copy code

docs.title: Doubly Linked List (Java uses this)
docs.text:
null ← A ⇄ B ⇄ C ⇄ D → null

shell Copy code

docs.title: Circular Linked List
docs.text:
A → B → C → A

yaml Copy code

docs.title: 4. Java LinkedList Class
docs.text:
public class LinkedList<E>
    extends AbstractSequentialList<E>
    implements List<E>, Deque<E>, Queue<E>

LinkedList can act as: - List - Queue - Deque - Stack (not recommended)

docs.title: Node Class (Simplified)
docs.text:
private static class Node<E> {
    E item;
    Node<E> next;
    Node<E> prev;
}

LinkedList Maintains

Node<E> first; // head
Node<E> last;  // tail
int size;

docs.title: 6. Visual Representation
docs.text:
first                         last
 ↓                             ↓
null ← A ⇄ B ⇄ C ⇄ D → null

Each node knows: - Its previous node - Its next node

docs.title: 7. Indexing in LinkedList (CRITICAL CONCEPT)
docs.text:
Does LinkedList have indexing? ✔ Logically – YES ❌ Physically – NO

Reason:

LinkedList implements List

So index-based methods exist:

java Copy code get(index) add(index, element) remove(index) But internally:

There is no array

No direct index-to-memory mapping

How get(index) works internally java Copy code list.get(5); Steps:

Index is validated

JVM decides traversal direction:

java Copy code if (index < size / 2) traverse from head; else traverse from tail; Moves node-by-node until index is reached

⏱ Time Complexity: O(n)

docs.title: 8. Why Indexing Is Slow in LinkedList
docs.text:
• Requires traversal
  • Pointer dereferencing
  • No cache locality
  • Nodes scattered in memory

📌 Note: Indexing exists only for API consistency.

docs.title: ➕ Add at End
docs.text:
list.add("A");

Steps:
- Create new node
- Set newNode.prev = last
- Set last.next = newNode
- Update last

⏱ Time Complexity: O(1)

Requires traversal

docs.title: 15. Time Complexity Summary (LinkedList)
docs.text: Operation Time Complexity get(index) O(n) addFirst() / addLast() O(1) removeFirst() / removeLast() O(1) add(index) O(n) remove(index) O(n)

docs.title: ✅ Use when:
docs.text:
• Frequent insert/remove at head or tail Example: Implementing an undo/redo feature where elements are added and removed from ends.

  • Queue / Deque use cases Example: Task scheduling systems, printer queues, or BFS traversal using a queue.

  • Size changes frequently Example: Applications where elements are dynamically added/removed, such as playlist management.

docs.title: ❌ Avoid when:
docs.text:
• Frequent random access Example: Accessing elements by index in a loop (list.get(i)), such as searching or sorting.

  • Read-heavy operations Example: Displaying large lists repeatedly (e.g., product catalogs).

  • Large datasets Example: Storing millions of elements where memory overhead and cache misses impact performance.

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature LinkedList ArrayList Internal DS Doubly Linked List Dynamic Array Indexing Logical only Physical get(index) O(n) O(1) Insert / Delete Fast at ends Slow in middle Memory High Low Cache Friendly No Yes

docs.title: ✅ ArrayList
docs.text:
Advantages - Fast random access (O(1)) - Better cache locality - Less memory overhead - Performs well for read-heavy operations

Disadvantages - Slow insertions/deletions in the middle - Resizing cost when capacity grows - Shifting elements is expensive

docs.title: ✅ LinkedList
docs.text:
Advantages - Fast insertions/deletions at beginning and end - No resizing overhead - Good for frequent structural modifications

Disadvantages - Slow random access (O(n)) - Higher memory usage (extra node pointers) - Poor cache performance

docs.title: Real-World Use Cases
docs.text: Scenario Preferred Collection Frequent random access ArrayList Read-heavy applications ArrayList Queue / Deque implementation LinkedList Frequent insert/delete at ends LinkedList Memory-sensitive applications ArrayList Large data with frequent updates LinkedList

docs.title: 📌 Quick Recommendation
docs.text:
• Use ArrayList by default
  • Use LinkedList only when:
  • Insertions/deletions at ends dominate
  • Random access is rare

docs.title: 18. Interview-Ready Explanation (Memorize This)
docs.text: LinkedList in Java is implemented as a doubly linked list where each element is stored as a node containing references to the previous and next nodes. Although it supports index-based operations through the List interface, it does not provide direct indexing internally, and accessing elements requires traversal, making get operations O(n). LinkedList is best suited for scenarios involving frequent insertions and deletions at the ends, such as queues and deques.

docs.title: 19. Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Doubly linked list implementation
  • No physical indexing
  • No shifting of elements
  • High memory overhead
  • Poor cache locality
  • Best for queue/deque scenarios

docs.title: HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs TreeMap
🎯 Why do we even need Map?
docs.text:
List and Set store only values.

But real-world applications require:

key → value

• userId → User
  • accountNo → Balance

docs.title: ✅ What is Map?
docs.text:
A Map stores data in:

<Key, Value>

docs.text:
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("A", 10);

🧠 How to Choose
docs.text:
Always decide based on behavior:

  • More reading → ArrayList
  • More insert/delete → LinkedList

docs.text:
Index →   0    1    2    3

  • Very fast random access O(1)
  • Insert/delete costly (shifting)

docs.title: LinkedList (Nodes)
docs.text:
[A|next] → [B|next] → [C|next] → [D|null]
  • Non‑continuous memory
  • Fast insert/delete O(1)
  • Slow random access O(n)
  • Extra memory for pointers

List<Transaction> transactions = new ArrayList<>();

List<WebElement> rows = driver.findElements(By.xpath("//table/tbody/tr"));

for(WebElement row : rows){

Queue-style execution

docs.text:
push(A)
push(B)
push(C)

Stack:

| C |  ← pop()
| B |
| A |
-----

After pop() → C removed first

docs.title: Internal Working
docs.text:
Stack extends Vector:

Stack → Vector → Object[]

Internally:

Object[] elementData int size

docs.title: push()
docs.text: elementData[size++] = item

docs.title: pop()
docs.text:
return elementData[--size]

Time Complexity → O(1)

stack.push("Java");

docs.title: 🚀 Custom Exceptions in Selenium – Complete Notes
🔴 The Big Question
docs.text: ❓ If Selenium and Java already provide many exceptions, why do we need custom exceptions?

docs.title: ✅ Short Answer
docs.text: Built-in exceptions tell WHAT failed, Custom exceptions tell WHY it failed in business/framework context.

docs.title: 🧠 Why Selenium Built-in Exceptions Are NOT Enough
docs.text:
Selenium exceptions like:

  • NoSuchElementException
  • TimeoutException
  • ElementNotInteractableException

tell only technical failure, not intent or meaning.

docs.title: ❌ Example (Confusing)
docs.text:
NoSuchElementException

Questions:

  • Login failed?
  • Wrong page?
  • User not created?
  • Locator issue?

❌ Not clear

docs.title: ✅ With Custom Exception (Clear)
docs.text:
LoginFailedException: User could not login due to invalid credentials

✔ Meaningful ✔ Readable ✔ Business-focused

docs.title: ✅ Why We Create Custom Exceptions
docs.text: Reason Benefit Business meaning Clear failure reason Framework clarity Easy debugging Reusability Same exception across tests Clean code No duplicate error handling Better reports Meaningful logs Interview expectation Senior-level design

docs.title: 🧩 Types of Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
You can create:

1️⃣ Checked custom exception 2️⃣ Runtime (Unchecked) custom exception

docs.title: 🔹 1️⃣ Custom Runtime Exception (Most common in Selenium)
When to use
docs.text: ✔ Test failure ✔ Validation failure ✔ Framework misuse

docs.title: Step 1: Create Custom Exception Class
docs.text:
public class LoginFailedException extends RuntimeException {

    public LoginFailedException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

✔ Extends RuntimeException ✔ No need to force handling

docs.title: Step 2: Throw Custom Exception (throw)
docs.text:
public void login(String user, String pass) {

    if(user == null || pass == null) {
        throw new LoginFailedException("Username or Password is null");
    }

    // Selenium logic
}

docs.title: Step 3: Use in Selenium Test
docs.text:
@Test
public void loginTest() {

    loginPage.login(null, "password123");
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
LoginFailedException: Username or Password is null

✔ Clear ✔ Actionable

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: ✔ External dependency ✔ Configuration issue ✔ Mandatory handling

docs.title: Step 1: Create Checked Exception
docs.text:
public class BrowserNotSupportedException extends Exception {

    public BrowserNotSupportedException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

docs.title: Step 2: Declare using throws
docs.text:
public void launchBrowser(String browser)
        throws BrowserNotSupportedException {

    if(!browser.equals("chrome")) {
        throw new BrowserNotSupportedException("Browser not supported");
    }
}

docs.title: Step 3: Handle using try-catch
docs.text:
try {
    launchBrowser("safari");
}
catch (BrowserNotSupportedException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getMessage());
}

docs.title: Scenario: Element not found after wait
❌ Bad practice
docs.text:
driver.findElement(By.id("login"));

Throws:

NoSuchElementException

docs.title: ✅ Good practice (Wrap with custom exception)
docs.text:
public WebElement findElement(By locator) {

    try {
        return wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(locator));
    }
    catch (TimeoutException e) {
        throw new ElementNotVisibleException(
            "Element not visible: " + locator.toString());
    }
}

docs.title: Custom Exception
docs.text:
public class ElementNotVisibleException extends RuntimeException {

    public ElementNotVisibleException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
ElementNotVisibleException: Element not visible: id=loginBtn

✔ Clear failure ✔ Better report ✔ Faster debugging

docs.title: 🔁 How Custom Exceptions Flow in Framework
docs.text:
Low-level Selenium action
        ↓
throw CustomException
        ↓
Test layer (JUnit/TestNG)
        ↓
Report + Screenshot + Fail test

docs.title: 🏗️ Where to Place Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
Best practice:

src/main/java
 └── exceptions
      ├── LoginFailedException.java
      ├── ElementNotVisibleException.java
      ├── BrowserNotSupportedException.java

docs.title: 🔹 throw vs throws in Custom Exceptions
docs.text: Keyword Usage throw Create custom exception throws Declare responsibility

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public void openPage() throws PageLoadException {
    throw new PageLoadException("Page load failed");
}

docs.title: Option 1: Let Test Fail (Recommended)
docs.text:
throw new LoginFailedException("Login failed");

✔ Test fails ✔ Clear reason

docs.title: Option 2: Catch and Log
docs.text:
try {
    login();
}
catch(LoginFailedException e) {
    logger.error(e.getMessage());
    throw e; // rethrow
}

docs.title: ❌ When NOT to Create Custom Exception
docs.text: ❌ For every small issue ❌ For simple NullPointer ❌ Overengineering

docs.title: 🎯 Interview GOLD Explanation
docs.text: “Although Selenium provides many exceptions, they are technical. Custom exceptions help represent business and framework-level failures clearly. They improve readability, debugging, reusability, and reporting, especially in large automation frameworks.”

docs.title: ✅ Interview One-Liner
docs.text: “Custom exceptions in Selenium provide meaningful, domain-specific error messages and help separate technical failures from business logic, making automation frameworks more maintainable.”

docs.title: 🧠 Memory Trick
docs.text:
Built-in exception → WHAT failed
Custom exception   → WHY it failed

END

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An Exception is an unexpected event that disrupts the normal flow of a program.

Examples:

  • Divide by zero
  • File not found
  • Null pointer access
  • DB connection failure

docs.title: ✅ Exception Hierarchy (Diagram)
docs.text:
Object
   ↓
Throwable
   ├── Error                  (Serious, system level)
   │     ├── OutOfMemoryError
   │     ├── StackOverflowError

   └── Exception              (Application level)
         ├── Checked Exceptions (Compile time)
         │      ├── IOException

         └── RuntimeException (Unchecked)
                ├── NullPointerException
                ├── ArithmeticException
                ├── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
                ├── IllegalArgumentException
                └── NumberFormatException

docs.title: ✅ Throwable
docs.text:
Root class of all errors and exceptions.

Two main types:

  • Error
  • Exception

docs.title: Description
docs.text: System-level failures. Not meant to be handled by application code.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• OutOfMemoryError
  • StackOverflowError

docs.title: Handling?
docs.text: ❌ Usually NOT handled

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Application-level issues that can be handled.

Two types:

  • Checked
  • Runtime

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Checked by compiler. Must handle using:

  • try-catch OR
  • throws

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• IOException
  • SQLException
  • FileNotFoundException

docs.title: Example
docs.text: FileReader f = new FileReader("test.txt"); // compile error if not handled

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Occur during execution. Compiler does NOT force handling.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• NullPointerException
  • ArithmeticException
  • IndexOutOfBoundsException

docs.title: Example
docs.text: int a = 10 / 0; // runtime crash

docs.title: 🔥 Checked vs Runtime (Interview Table)
docs.text: Feature Checked Runtime Checked by Compiler JVM Handling required Yes No Occurs Compile time Runtime Cause External issues Coding mistakes Example IOException NullPointer

docs.title: Easy Memory
docs.text:
Checked → outside problems (file/db/network)
Runtime → coding mistakes

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
try {
   risky code
}
catch(Exception e){
   handle
}
finally{
   cleanup
}

docs.title: ✅ try Block
docs.text:
Contains code that may throw exception.

try {
    int a = 10/0;
}

docs.title: ✅ catch Block
docs.text:
Handles exception.

catch(ArithmeticException e){
    System.out.println("Divide by zero");
}

docs.title: ✅ Multiple Catch (YES allowed)
docs.text:
try {
    int a = 10/0;
}
catch(ArithmeticException e){
    System.out.println("Math error");
}
catch(NullPointerException e){
    System.out.println("Null error");
}
catch(Exception e){
    System.out.println("Generic error");
}

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
Always:

Specific → General

docs.title: ✅ Multi-Catch (Java 7+)
docs.text:
catch(IOException | SQLException e){
    System.out.println("DB or IO error");
}

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Always executes (exception or not).

docs.title: Used for
docs.text:
• Close DB
  • Close file
  • Cleanup
  • Release resources

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
finally{
   System.out.println("Always runs");
}

docs.title: finally does NOT run if
docs.text:
• System.exit()
  • JVM crash
  • Power failure

docs.title: ✅ Can we write only try?
docs.text:
❌ No

Must have:

try + catch OR try + finally

docs.title: throw (manual exception)
docs.text:
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid age");

Used to explicitly throw exception.

docs.title: throws (delegate exception)
docs.text:
public void readFile() throws IOException {
}

Caller must handle.

try {
    driver.findElement(By.id("login")).click();
}
catch(NoSuchElementException e){

}
finally{

docs.title: ✅ Best Practices
docs.text: ✔ Handle only where needed ✔ Use specific exceptions ✔ Always cleanup resources ✔ Avoid empty catch blocks ✔ Log errors ✔ Prefer try-with-resources

docs.text: Yes

docs.title: ✅ Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Throwable
   ├── Error
   └── Exception
         ├── Checked

try → risky
catch → handle
finally → cleanup

docs.title: 🎯 One-Line Interview Answer
docs.text:
"Java exceptions extend Throwable and are divided into Error and Exception. Exceptions are further classified into checked and runtime. Checked must be handled at compile time, while runtime occur during execution. We handle them using try-catch-finally."

END

docs.title: 🚀 Java Exception Handling – Why throw and throws when we already have try–catch?
🔴 First: The CORE Confusion
docs.text:
You might think:

❓ “If I already have try–catch to handle exceptions, why do I need throw and throws?”

docs.title: ✅ One-line Answer
docs.text:
try–catch → handles exception HERE
throw     → CREATES an exception
throws    → PASSES responsibility to CALLER

👉 They solve different problems, not the same one.

docs.title: 🧠 Think in TERMS OF RESPONSIBILITY
docs.text: Exception handling is about:

docs.title: 👉 WHO is responsible?
docs.text:
There are 3 possibilities:

Situation Keyword I will handle it here try–catch I detect a problem and want to report it throw I cannot handle it here throws

docs.title: ✅ Why try–catch alone is NOT enough
❌ Problem with try–catch everywhere
docs.text:
If you do this everywhere:

try {
   readFile();
} catch (Exception e) {
   e.printStackTrace();
}

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: ❌ code becomes messy ❌ business logic + error handling mixed ❌ lower-level methods decide behavior ❌ not reusable ❌ breaks clean architecture

docs.title: ✅ Solution
docs.text:
Java gives:

  • throw
  • throws

to separate concerns.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Manually create and signal a problem when business rules fail

docs.title: Example (Business rule failure)
docs.text:
int age = -5;

Java will NOT throw error automatically.

But logically:

❌ Invalid age

docs.title: Solution → throw
docs.text:
if (age < 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
}

docs.title: Key Point
docs.text: ✔ Not system error ✔ Your business rule

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: throw = YOU decide something is wrong

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Declare: “I cannot handle this exception here”

Used in:

✔ utility methods ✔ service layer ✔ DAO layer ✔ low-level code

docs.title: WITHOUT throws (compile error)
docs.text:
public void readFile() {
    FileReader fr = new FileReader("a.txt"); // ❌ compile error
}

Java says:

Handle it OR declare it

docs.title: WITH throws
docs.text:
public void readFile() throws IOException {
    FileReader fr = new FileReader("a.txt");
}

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: 👉 Caller must handle it

docs.title: Rule
docs.text: throws = pass responsibility upward

docs.title: 🔥 How ALL THREE work together (REAL FLOW)
docs.text: Let’s see real project style architecture.

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ Low-level method → throws
docs.text:
public void readFile() throws IOException {
    FileReader fr = new FileReader("data.txt");
}

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: This method cannot decide what to do if file missing.

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ Business logic → throw
docs.text:
public void processUser(int age) throws IOException {

    if (age < 18) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("User not eligible");
    }

    readFile();
}

docs.title: Here
docs.text: ✔ throw → business validation ✔ throws → technical delegation

docs.title: Step 3️⃣ Top-level → try–catch
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {

    try {
        processUser(15);
    }
    catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        System.out.println("Business error: " + e.getMessage());
    }
    catch (IOException e) {
        System.out.println("Technical error: file missing");
    }
}

docs.title: 🏗️ Real-world Layering (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text: Layer Uses Utility / DAO throws Business logic throw Controller / Test / UI try–catch

docs.title: 🔥 Visual Flow Diagram
docs.text:
Low Level (DAO)
    ↓
throws IOException
    ↓
Business Layer
    ↓
throw BusinessException
    ↓
Controller / Main
    ↓
try–catch handles everything

docs.title: 🔹 Key Differences
docs.text: Aspect throw throws try–catch Purpose create exception declare exception handle exception Location inside method method signature caller block Responsibility caller handles caller handles handled here Usage business validation technical delegation recovery

docs.title: 🔹 When to use what?
docs.text: Situation Use Invalid input throw Cannot handle exception throws Want to recover/log/show message try–catch

docs.title: 🔹 Simple Memory Trick
docs.text:
throw  → create
throws → declare
try    → test
catch  → handle
finally→ cleanup

docs.title: 🎯 Interview GOLD Explanation
docs.text: “We don’t use try–catch everywhere because it mixes logic and handling. throw is used to explicitly raise business problems. throws is used to delegate exception handling to the caller. try–catch is used only where the application can actually decide how to recover.”

docs.title: ✅ Final One-Line Summary
docs.text:
throw   → create problem
throws  → pass problem
try-catch → solve problem

END

docs.title: 🚀 Wrapper Classes in Java – Complete Notes
Definition
docs.text:
Wrapper classes are Java classes that convert primitive data types into objects.

They “wrap” a primitive value inside an object.

docs.title: Primitive → Wrapper Mapping
docs.text: Primitive Wrapper Class byte Byte short Short int Integer long Long float Float double Double char Character boolean Boolean

docs.title: 🔴 Why Do We Need Wrapper Classes?
docs.text:
This is the most important question.

❓ If primitives already exist, why wrapper classes?

Because many Java features work only with objects, not primitives.

docs.title: 🔹 1️⃣ Collections Work Only with Objects (Most Important)
❌ Invalid (Primitive not allowed)
docs.text: ArrayList<int> list = new ArrayList<>(); // compile-time error

docs.title: ✅ Valid (Wrapper)
docs.text:
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(10);

👉 Collections store object references, not primitive values.

docs.title: 🔹 2️⃣ Generics Support Only Objects
docs.text:
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
List<Double> prices = new ArrayList<>();

Primitives cannot be used with generics.

docs.title: Primitive (Not allowed)
docs.text: int a = null; // ❌ error

docs.title: Wrapper (Allowed)
docs.text:
Integer a = null; // ✅

Very useful in:

  • Database values
  • API responses
  • Optional fields

docs.title: 🔹 4️⃣ Utility Methods Provided
docs.text: Wrapper classes provide many useful methods.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Integer.parseInt("100");
Double.parseDouble("10.5");
Boolean.parseBoolean("true");

Primitives cannot do this.

docs.title: 🔹 5️⃣ Object-Oriented Features
docs.text:
Wrapper classes:

  • Are objects
  • Have methods
  • Can be passed as references
  • Can be used in frameworks

Primitives:

  • Store only values
  • No methods

docs.title: 🔹 Autoboxing
docs.text:
Automatically converts primitive → wrapper.

int x = 10;
Integer obj = x;   // autoboxing

Internally:

Integer obj = Integer.valueOf(10);

docs.title: 🔹 Unboxing
docs.text:
Automatically converts wrapper → primitive.

Integer obj = 20;
int y = obj;   // unboxing

Internally:

int y = obj.intValue();

docs.title: 🔹 Example Code
docs.text:
public class WrapperDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        int a = 5;

        // Autoboxing
        Integer obj = a;

        // Unboxing
        int b = obj;

        System.out.println(obj + " " + b);
    }
}

docs.title: 🟢 Example 1: Collections
docs.text:
List<Integer> marks = new ArrayList<>();
marks.add(90);
marks.add(85);

docs.title: 🟢 Example 2: Selenium / Test Data
docs.text:
Map<String, Integer> userAge = new HashMap<>();
userAge.put("Nitin", 28);

docs.title: 🟢 Example 3: API / JSON POJO
docs.text:
private Integer age;

Why not int? 👉 API may return null.

docs.title: 🟢 Example 4: Database Values
docs.text:
Integer salary = resultSet.getInt("salary");

Database fields can be null.

docs.title: Integer
docs.text:
Integer.parseInt("123");
Integer.valueOf(10);
Integer.max(5, 10);

docs.title: Double
docs.text: Double.parseDouble("99.5");

docs.title: Boolean
docs.text: Boolean.parseBoolean("true");

docs.title: 🔥 Primitive vs Wrapper (Interview Table)
docs.text: Feature Primitive Wrapper Data type Value Object Speed Faster Slower Memory Less More Supports null ❌ ✅ Methods ❌ ✅ Collections ❌ ✅ Generics ❌ ✅

docs.title: ❓ Why Not Always Use Wrapper Classes?
docs.text:
Because wrapper classes:

  • Consume more memory
  • Are slower than primitives
  • Create unnecessary objects

docs.title: ✔ Use Primitive When:
docs.text:
• Simple calculations
  • Performance is critical
  • Local variables
int sum = a + b;

docs.title: ✔ Use Wrapper When:
docs.text:
• Working with collections
  • Using generics
  • Handling null values
  • Reading DB / API data
  • Using utility methods
Integer count = null;

docs.title: Q1. Why are wrapper classes needed?
docs.text: Collections and generics work only with objects.

docs.title: Q2. What is autoboxing?
docs.text: Automatic conversion of primitive to wrapper.

docs.title: Q3. Difference between int and Integer?
docs.text: int is primitive, Integer is an object.

docs.title: Q4. Can wrapper classes be null?
docs.text: Yes.

docs.title: Q5. Which is faster – primitive or wrapper?
docs.text: Primitive.

docs.title: 🧠 Easy Memory Trick
docs.text:
Primitive → Fast
Wrapper   → Flexible

docs.title: 🎯 Interview One-Liner
docs.text:
“Wrapper classes allow primitive data types to be used as objects so they can work with collections, generics, and APIs. They also provide utility methods and support null values, which primitives cannot.”

END
