docs.text:
package utils;

import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.util.Properties;

public class ConfigManager {

    private static Properties prop = new Properties();

    // load config file once
    static {
        try {
            prop.load(new FileInputStream("src/test/resources/config.properties"));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println("config.properties not found");
        }
    }

    // CLI > config
    public static String get(String key) {
        String cli = System.getProperty(key);

        if (cli != null && !cli.isEmpty()) {
            return cli;
        }

        return prop.getProperty(key);
    }

    public static int getInt(String key) {
        return Integer.parseInt(get(key));
    }

    public static boolean getBoolean(String key) {
        return Boolean.parseBoolean(get(key));
    }
}

docs.title: 🧠 Override Logic Explained
docs.text:
System.getProperty(key, prop.getProperty(key));

Priority:

CLI (-D)  → highest
config file → fallback
hardcoded → last

docs.title: ✅ Step 3 — DriverFactory
docs.text:
package factory;

import utils.ConfigManager;
import org.openqa.selenium.*;
import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.*;
import org.openqa.selenium.firefox.FirefoxDriver;

import java.time.Duration;

public class DriverFactory {

    private static ThreadLocal<WebDriver> driver = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public static void initDriver() {

        String browser = ConfigManager.get("browser");
        boolean headless = ConfigManager.getBoolean("headless");
        int timeout = ConfigManager.getInt("timeout");

        switch (browser.toLowerCase()) {

            case "chrome":
                ChromeOptions options = new ChromeOptions();
                if (headless) options.addArguments("--headless=new");
                driver.set(new ChromeDriver(options));
                break;

            case "firefox":
                driver.set(new FirefoxDriver());
                break;

            default:
                throw new RuntimeException("Invalid browser: " + browser);
        }

        driver.get().manage().window().maximize();
        driver.get().manage().timeouts().implicitlyWait(Duration.ofSeconds(timeout));
    }

    public static WebDriver getDriver() {
        return driver.get();
    }

    public static void quitDriver() {
        driver.get().quit();
        driver.remove();
    }
}

docs.title: ⭐ Step 3 — Factory Pattern (DriverFactory) in Selenium Framework
🧠 Why did Factory come into picture?
docs.text: Let’s first see the common beginner approach.

docs.title: ❌ Without Factory
docs.text:
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();

Problem?

If tomorrow you want Firefox:

WebDriver driver = new FirefoxDriver();

Now imagine:

  • 150 test classes
  • Chrome hardcoded everywhere
  • Need cross-browser testing

💥 You must update 150 files manually.

docs.title: 🎯 Core Idea of Factory (1 line)
docs.text:
Move object creation logic into one central place.

Instead of tests creating drivers… Factory creates drivers.

docs.title: ✅ DriverFactory Example
docs.text:
public class DriverFactory {

    public static WebDriver createDriver(String browser) {

        WebDriver driver;

        switch (browser.toLowerCase()) {

            case "firefox":
                driver = new FirefoxDriver();
                break;

            case "edge":
                driver = new EdgeDriver();
                break;

            default:
                driver = new ChromeDriver();
        }

        return driver;
    }
}

docs.title: ✅ Usage
docs.text: WebDriver driver = DriverFactory.createDriver("chrome");

docs.title: ⭐ Professional Version (Factory + Singleton + ThreadLocal)
docs.text:
public class DriverFactory {

    public static void initDriver(String browser) {

        WebDriver driver;

        switch (browser.toLowerCase()) {

            case "firefox":
                driver = new FirefoxDriver();
                break;

            default:
                driver = new ChromeDriver();
        }

        DriverManager.setDriver(driver);
    }
}

docs.title: ✅ Flow
docs.text: Test → BaseTest → DriverFactory → DriverManager → ThreadLocal

docs.title: ✅ Rule
docs.text: Never create drivers directly in tests. Always use DriverFactory.

docs.title: ⭐ Step 1 — Page Object Model (POM) in Selenium Framework
🧠 Why did POM come into picture?
docs.text: Early Selenium tests directly interacted with WebDriver inside test methods.

docs.title: ❌ Without POM
docs.text:
@Test
public void loginTest() {
    driver.findElement(By.id("username")).sendKeys("admin");
    driver.findElement(By.id("password")).sendKeys("123");
    driver.findElement(By.id("loginBtn")).click();
}

Looks fine for 1–2 tests…

But imagine:

  • 200+ tests
  • Same login steps repeated
  • Locator changes

💥 Result → update 200 files manually

docs.title: 🚨 Problems Without POM
docs.text:
• ❌ Tight coupling between test & UI
  • ❌ Duplicate code
  • ❌ Hard maintenance
  • ❌ Poor readability
  • ❌ Not scalable

docs.title: 🎯 Core Idea of POM (1 line)
docs.text:
Each web page = one Java class

Tests should NOT talk directly to Selenium. Tests should talk to Page methods.

docs.title: Tests should NEVER do:
docs.text: driver.findElement()

docs.title: Tests should ALWAYS do:

docs.title: LoginPage.java
docs.text:
package pages;

import org.openqa.selenium.By;
import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver;

public class LoginPage {

    WebDriver driver;

    private By username = By.id("user");
    private By password = By.id("pass");
    private By loginBtn = By.id("login");

    public LoginPage(WebDriver driver) {
        this.driver = driver;
    }

    public void enterUsername(String user) {
        driver.findElement(username).sendKeys(user);
    }

    public void enterPassword(String pass) {
        driver.findElement(password).sendKeys(pass);
    }

    public void clickLogin() {
        driver.findElement(loginBtn).click();
    }

    public void login(String user, String pass) {
        enterUsername(user);
        enterPassword(pass);
        clickLogin();
    }
}

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Answer
docs.text: POM separates UI locators and page actions from tests. It improves maintainability, readability, and reusability while reducing duplication.

docs.text: ❌ driver.findElement() inside tests

docs.title: Always:
docs.text: ✅ page methods

docs.title: Problem (Without Singleton)
docs.text:
If every test creates its own driver like this:

WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();

Problems:

  • Multiple browsers open unexpectedly
  • Memory waste
  • Session conflicts
  • Hard to manage lifecycle
  • Driver created in many places

When the framework grows (100+ tests), this becomes chaos.

docs.title: 🎯 Core Idea of Singleton (1 line)
docs.text:
Allow ONLY ONE instance of a class in the entire framework.

For Selenium:

👉 Only ONE WebDriver per execution (or per thread).

docs.title: DriverManager.java
docs.text:
public class DriverManager {

    private static WebDriver driver;

    private DriverManager() {}

    public static WebDriver getDriver() {

        if (driver == null) {
            driver = new ChromeDriver();
        }

        return driver;
    }

    public static void quitDriver() {
        if (driver != null) {
            driver.quit();
            driver = null;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: WebDriver driver = DriverManager.getDriver();

docs.title: ✅ What Singleton Solves
docs.text:
• ✅ Single driver instance
  • ✅ Centralized control
  • ✅ Easy lifecycle management
  • ✅ Memory efficient
  • ✅ Avoid duplicate drivers

docs.title: ⚠️ But Wait… What About Parallel Execution?
docs.text:
Good question 👍

If you run parallel tests and still use the above Singleton:

❌ All threads share SAME driver ❌ Tests overwrite each other ❌ Random failures

So classic Singleton is NOT enough.

docs.title: ⭐ Modern Solution → Singleton + ThreadLocal
docs.text:
In real Selenium frameworks, we combine:

👉 Singleton (one instance manager) 👉 ThreadLocal (one driver per thread)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Parallel tests:

Thread 1 → Chrome Thread 2 → Firefox

If driver is global:

driver = Chrome
driver = Firefox

Both threads fight for same object.

docs.title: ThreadLocal Concept
docs.text:
Each thread gets its own copy of variable

So:

Thread 1 → Driver A Thread 2 → Driver B Thread 3 → Driver C

Perfect isolation.

docs.title: DriverManager.java
docs.text:
public class DriverManager {

    private static ThreadLocal<WebDriver> driver = new ThreadLocal<>();

    private DriverManager() {}

    public static WebDriver getDriver() {
        return driver.get();
    }

    public static void setDriver(WebDriver driverInstance) {
        driver.set(driverInstance);
    }

    public static void quitDriver() {
        driver.get().quit();
        driver.remove();
    }
}

docs.title: DriverFactory.java
docs.text:
public class DriverFactory {

    public static void initDriver(String browser) {

        WebDriver driver;

        switch(browser) {
            case "firefox":
                driver = new FirefoxDriver();
                break;

            default:
                driver = new ChromeDriver();
        }

        DriverManager.setDriver(driver);
    }
}

docs.title: BaseTest.java
docs.text:
@BeforeMethod
public void setup() {
    DriverFactory.initDriver("chrome");
}

@AfterMethod
public void tearDown() {
    DriverManager.quitDriver();
}

docs.title: 🎯 Now What Happens?
docs.text:
If threadCount = 3:

Thread 1 → Chrome
Thread 2 → Chrome
Thread 3 → Chrome

Each has separate driver.

✅ Safe parallel execution.

docs.title: 🧠 So Why Still Call It Singleton?
docs.text: Great confusion point 👍

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
We are NOT making WebDriver Singleton.

We are making:

👉 DriverManager Singleton

Meaning:

  • Only ONE manager class
  • Centralized access point
  • But drivers stored per thread

So:

Singleton manager
    ↓
ThreadLocal drivers

docs.text: Feature Singleton Only ThreadLocal Only Singleton + ThreadLocal (Best) Single control point ❌ ❌ ✅ Parallel safe ❌ ✅ ✅ Central lifecycle ❌ ❌ ✅ Industry usage ❌ ❌ ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

👉 Why use Singleton when ThreadLocal exists?

You say:

Singleton gives centralized driver management, while ThreadLocal provides thread safety. Together they allow one driver per thread with controlled lifecycle. This is the industry-standard approach for parallel Selenium frameworks.

docs.title: Never:
docs.text: ❌ new ChromeDriver() inside tests

docs.title: Always:
docs.text: ✅ DriverManager.getDriver()

docs.title: 🚀 Final Takeaway
docs.text:
Use:

Singleton → Manage ThreadLocal → Isolate Factory → Create

These 3 together build a professional driver architecture.

docs.title: ⭐ Step 4 — Template Method Pattern (BaseTest) in Selenium Framework
🧠 Why did Template Method come into picture?
docs.text: Let’s see a common beginner mistake.

docs.title: ❌ Without BaseTest
docs.text:
Every test class repeats setup and teardown.

public class LoginTest {

    WebDriver driver;

    @BeforeMethod
    public void setup() {
        driver = new ChromeDriver();
        driver.manage().window().maximize();
    }

    @AfterMethod
    public void teardown() {
        driver.quit();
    }
}

Now imagine:

  • 50 test classes
  • Same setup/teardown copied everywhere
  • Want to add logging or config

💥 You must update 50 files manually.

docs.title: 🚨 Problems Without Template Method
docs.text:
• ❌ Duplicate setup code
  • ❌ Hard maintenance
  • ❌ Inconsistent configuration
  • ❌ Poor scalability
  • ❌ Violation of DRY principle

docs.title: 🎯 Core Idea of Template Method (1 line)
docs.text:
Define test execution flow once in a parent class and reuse it everywhere.

We create:

👉 One BaseTest 👉 All tests extend it

docs.title: BaseTest.java
docs.text:
import org.testng.annotations.AfterMethod;
import org.testng.annotations.BeforeMethod;

public class BaseTest {

    @BeforeMethod
    public void setup() {

        String browser = System.getProperty("browser", "chrome");

        DriverFactory.initDriver(browser);

        DriverManager.getDriver().manage().window().maximize();
    }

    @AfterMethod
    public void teardown() {

        DriverManager.quitDriver();
    }
}

docs.title: LoginTest.java
docs.text:
public class LoginTest extends BaseTest {

    @Test
    public void loginTest() {

        LoginPage loginPage = new LoginPage(DriverManager.getDriver());

        loginPage.login("admin", "123");
    }
}

docs.title: 🎯 Benefits
docs.text:
• ✅ Setup written once
  • ✅ Clean tests
  • ✅ Easy maintenance
  • ✅ Consistent lifecycle
  • ✅ Highly scalable

docs.title: 🎯 Flow
docs.text: TestNG → BaseTest.setup() → Test → BaseTest.teardown()

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Answer
docs.text: Template Method defines a fixed execution flow in a parent class. All tests inherit it to reuse setup and teardown logic, keeping tests clean and maintainable.

docs.title: ✅ Rule
docs.text: Never setup driver inside each test. Always extend BaseTest.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Explain TestNG Architecture. Why is it better than JUnit?
✅ Concept
docs.text:
TestNG is a testing framework built on top of Java Reflection + Annotations + XML configuration.

It works like this internally:

  • Reads testng.xml
  • Scans classes using Reflection
  • Finds annotations (@Test, @BeforeMethod, etc.)
  • Builds execution plan
  • Executes methods in order
  • Generates reports

docs.title: ✅ Architecture Flow
docs.text:
testng.xml
     ↓
Suite Parser
     ↓
Annotation Scanner (Reflection)
     ↓
Dependency Resolver
     ↓
Thread Pool Manager
     ↓
Test Executor
     ↓
Listeners / Reports

docs.title: ✅ Why TestNG is better than JUnit?
docs.text: Feature TestNG JUnit Parallel execution ✅ Native ❌ Limited testng.xml ✅ Yes ❌ No Dependency management ✅ Yes ❌ No Groups ✅ Yes ❌ No DataProvider ✅ Powerful Limited Retry mechanism ✅ Built-in Manual Suite-level config ✅ Yes ❌ No

docs.title: ✅ Interview Line
docs.text: 👉 “TestNG is more suitable for large automation frameworks due to parallelism, grouping, dependency control and XML-driven execution.”

docs.title: 2️⃣ What is Lifecycle of TestNG Annotations?
✅ Concept
docs.text:
TestNG runs methods in a hierarchical execution order:

Suite → Test → Class → Method

Each level controls setup/cleanup scope.

docs.title: ✅ Execution Order
docs.text:
@BeforeSuite
   @BeforeTest
      @BeforeClass
         @BeforeMethod
            @Test
         @AfterMethod
      @AfterClass
   @AfterTest
@AfterSuite

docs.title: ✅ Example
docs.text:
@BeforeSuite
public void startSuite(){}

@BeforeClass
public void setupClass(){}

@BeforeMethod
public void setup(){}

@Test
public void testLogin(){}

@AfterMethod
public void cleanup(){}

docs.title: 👉 S → T → C → M → Test → M → C → T → S

Supposewe have two classes and in both have same annotation example @BeforeSuite or @BeforeTest -> here Question is which one execute first-> internally it check which present more configs and it pick and run.
✅ Real Behavior (Important)
docs.text:
TestNG does NOT use class/XML order for:

  • @BeforeSuite
  • @BeforeTest
  • @AfterTest
  • @AfterSuite

Instead it uses:

Lifecycle stage → internal grouping → internal sorting (On sorting bases it decde which has more configs it runs)

docs.title: ✅ Practical Meaning
docs.text: Annotation Scope Use Case BeforeSuite Whole suite Reports, DB connection BeforeTest Per  block Browser launch BeforeClass Per class Page objects setup BeforeMethod Per test Login, reset data AfterMethod Per test Cleanup AfterSuite End of suite Close reports ---

docs.title: 🎯 Quick Summary
docs.text:
• TestNG uses reflection + annotations + XML
  • Lifecycle is hierarchical
  • More powerful than JUnit
  • Best for large automation frameworks
  • Supports parallelism, grouping, dependencies, data-driven testing

docs.title: 📘 TestNG Dependency Guide — dependsOnMethods vs dependsOnGroups
🔹 Overview
docs.text:
TestNG provides two main dependency mechanisms:

  • dependsOnMethods → method level dependency
  • dependsOnGroups → group level dependency

They look similar but behave VERY differently internally.

Understanding this is critical for framework design + interviews + stable automation.

docs.title: ✅ Concept
docs.text:
Creates hard dependency between methods. Child runs ONLY if parent PASSES.

method → method

docs.title: ✅ Example (Same Class)
docs.text:
public class OrderTest {

    @Test
    public void login() {}

    @Test(dependsOnMethods = "login")
    public void placeOrder() {}
}

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: If parent fails → dependent is SKIPPED

docs.title: ❌ Limitation
docs.text:
Does NOT work across classes.

Reason: TestNG searches only inside SAME class when resolving dependsOnMethods.

docs.title: Use when
docs.text: Small flows inside the same class only.

docs.title: ✅ Concept
docs.text:
Creates dependency on GROUPS, not methods. Child runs only after ALL tests in group pass.

method → group

docs.title: ⭐ Important Rule
docs.text: 👉 Dependent runs only after ALL group tests finish

docs.title: Why it works across classes?
docs.text:
TestNG builds a global group map internally:

GroupName → List of all methods in that group

So it can resolve dependencies across any class.

docs.title: ✅ Cross-Class Example
docs.text:
LoginTest

@Test(groups = "cleanup")
public void cleanup() {}

OrderTest

@Test(dependsOnGroups = "cleanup")
public void placeOrder() {}

Execution: cleanup → placeOrder

docs.title: Multiple methods in group
docs.text: All must pass before dependent runs.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text: Any failure in group → dependent skipped.

docs.title: 🔵 Internal Working (Simplified)
docs.text:
1. Parse testng.xml
  2. Scan classes using reflection
  3. Collect annotations
  4. Build dependency graph (DAG)
  5. Topological sort
  6. Execute

docs.title: 🔵 Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature dependsOnMethods dependsOnGroups Scope method group Cross-class ❌ ✅ Target single method many methods Recommended limited ✅ best

docs.title: 🔵 Best Practices
docs.text: Avoid heavy test-to-test dependencies. Prefer: - independent tests - setup/cleanup in Before/After methods - groups for logical flows

docs.title: 🔵 Interview Lines
docs.text:
dependsOnMethods works only within same class. dependsOnGroups works globally across classes. For cross-class dependency always prefer dependsOnGroups.

docs.title: 📘 Extent Reports with TestNG — Complete Guide (From Scratch)
🔷 1️⃣ Concept — What is Extent Report?
docs.text:
Extent Reports is a rich HTML reporting library used with TestNG/Selenium that:

  • Captures test execution
  • Shows pass/fail/skip
  • Attaches screenshots
  • Displays charts & dashboards
  • Works with CI/CD

Default TestNG reports are basic and lack screenshots and visualization, so Extent is preferred in industry.

docs.title: 🔷 2️⃣ Types of Reporters
docs.text:
Reporter Output Use SparkReporter HTML Most common AventReporter JSON CI integration KlovReporter MongoDB Live dashboards EmailReporter Email Notifications

👉 Spark Reporter is used most frequently.

docs.text:
• attachReporter()
  • createTest()
  • flush()

docs.text:
• pass()
  • fail()
  • skip()
  • info()
  • addScreenCaptureFromPath()

docs.text:

  • setReportName()

   <groupId>com.aventstack</groupId>

docs.title: ExtentManager
docs.text:
public class ExtentManager {

    private static ExtentReports extent;

    public static ExtentReports getInstance(){

        if(extent == null){

            ExtentSparkReporter spark =
                new ExtentSparkReporter("target/extent-report.html");

            spark.config().setDocumentTitle("Automation Report");
            spark.config().setReportName("Regression Suite");
            spark.config().setTheme(Theme.DARK);

            extent = new ExtentReports();
            extent.attachReporter(spark);
        }

        return extent;
    }
}

docs.title: Screenshot Utility
docs.text:
public static String capture(String name) throws Exception {

    File src = ((TakesScreenshot)DriverFactory.getDriver())
            .getScreenshotAs(OutputType.FILE);

    new File("target/screenshots").mkdirs();

    String path = "target/screenshots/" + name + ".png";
    FileUtils.copyFile(src, new File(path));

    return "screenshots/" + name + ".png";
}

docs.title: Listener Integration
docs.text:
public class TestListener implements ITestListener {

    ExtentReports extent = ExtentManager.getInstance();
    ThreadLocal<ExtentTest> test = new ThreadLocal<>();

    public void onTestStart(ITestResult result){
        test.set(extent.createTest(result.getName()));
    }

    public void onTestSuccess(ITestResult result){
        test.get().pass("Passed");
    }

    public void onTestFailure(ITestResult result){
        String path = ScreenshotUtil.capture(result.getName());
        test.get().fail(result.getThrowable())
            .addScreenCaptureFromPath(path);
    }

    public void onTestSkipped(ITestResult result){
        test.get().skip("Skipped");
    }

    public void onFinish(ITestContext context){
        extent.flush();
    }
}

docs.title: testng.xml
docs.text:
<listeners>
   <listener class-name="listeners.TestListener"/>
</listeners>

or

@Listeners(TestListener.class)

@Test public void loginFail(){ Assert.fail(); }
@Test public void loginSkip(){ throw new SkipException("Skip"); }
@Test public void loginInfo(){ Assert.assertTrue(true); }

docs.title: 📘 TestNG Guide — invocationCount, threadPoolSize & Data-Driven Testing
🔹 Overview
docs.text:
In TestNG, we often need to:

✅ Run the same test multiple times ✅ Run tests concurrently (parallel) ✅ Run tests with different datasets

TestNG provides:

  • invocationCount → repeat test N times
  • threadPoolSize → run those repeats in parallel
  • DataProvider → run test with different data

Each serves a different purpose.

docs.title: ✅ Concept
docs.text:
Repeats the SAME test multiple times.

👉 Think: loop execution

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
@Test(invocationCount = 3)
public void testLoginAPI() {
    System.out.println("Running login API test");
}

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
Run
Run
Run

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• stress testing
  • retry logic
  • idempotency testing
  • repeated API calls

docs.title: ✅ Concept
docs.text: Runs invocations in parallel threads (must be used with invocationCount).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
@Test(invocationCount = 5, threadPoolSize = 2)
public void testPaymentAPI() {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getId());
}

docs.title: Execution (parallel)
docs.text:
Thread 11
Thread 12
Thread 11
Thread 12
Thread 11

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• concurrency testing
  • simulate multiple users
  • performance testing

⚠ Selenium Note: Use ThreadLocal for thread safety.

docs.title: 🔵 3️⃣ DataProvider — Run Test with Different Data
✅ Concept
docs.text:
Runs same test multiple times with different inputs.

👉 Think: parameterized testing

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
@DataProvider
public Object[][] users() {
    return new Object[][]{
        {"user1", "pass1"},
        {"user2", "pass2"}
    };
}

@Test(dataProvider = "users")
public void loginTest(String user, String pass) {
    System.out.println(user);
}

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
user1
user2

docs.title: 🔥 NEW — Cross Package DataProvider (Real Framework Use Case)
✅ Scenario
docs.text:
We have:

xyz package → DataProvider class
bny.erp package → Test class

We want to reuse common test data across packages.

docs.title: 📦 Package Structure
docs.text:
src/test/java
   ├─ xyz
   │     └─ TestDataProvider.java
   ├─ bny/erp
   │     └─ ERPLoginTest.java

docs.title: Step 1 — Create DataProvider in xyz package
xyz/TestDataProvider.java
docs.text:
package xyz;

import org.testng.annotations.DataProvider;

public class TestDataProvider {

    @DataProvider(name = "erpUsers")
    public static Object[][] erpUsers() {
        return new Object[][]{
            {"admin", "admin123"},
            {"manager", "manager123"},
            {"user", "user123"}
        };
    }
}

docs.title: bny/erp/ERPLoginTest.java
docs.text:
package bny.erp;

import org.testng.annotations.Test;
import xyz.TestDataProvider;

public class ERPLoginTest {

    @Test(dataProvider = "erpUsers", dataProviderClass = TestDataProvider.class)
    public void loginERP(String username, String password) {
        System.out.println(username + " -> " + password);
    }
}

docs.title: ✅ Important
docs.text:
When DataProvider is in DIFFERENT class/package:

You MUST use:

dataProviderClass = TestDataProvider.class

Otherwise TestNG cannot find it.

docs.title: 🔥 Execution Flow
docs.text:
TestNG internally:

  1. Finds test method
  2. Looks for provider in specified class
  3. Calls erpUsers()
  4. Creates 3 test invocations

docs.title: Execution Output
docs.text:
admin -> admin123
manager -> manager123
user -> user123

docs.title: ✅ Real Use Cases
docs.text:
• shared test data library
  • common login credentials
  • API payload sets
  • reusable across multiple modules
  • framework centralization

docs.title: 🔵 Parallel DataProvider
docs.text:
@DataProvider(name="erpUsers", parallel=true)

Runs each dataset in parallel.

docs.title: 🔵 Quick Comparison
docs.text: Requirement Solution Repeat same test invocationCount Repeat in parallel invocationCount + threadPoolSize Different inputs DataProvider Cross package reuse dataProviderClass Parallel different inputs DataProvider(parallel=true)

docs.title: 🔵 Best Practices
docs.text: ✅ Keep DataProviders in separate utility package ✅ Make them reusable ✅ Prefer DataProvider over invocationCount for data testing ✅ Use parallel=true for faster execution

docs.title: 🔵 Interview One-Liners
docs.text:
👉 invocationCount repeats test 👉 threadPoolSize runs repeats in parallel 👉 DataProvider runs same test with different data 👉 dataProviderClass allows cross-class/package reuse

docs.title: 🔁 TestNG Retry Mechanism (Test Level & Global Level)
docs.text:
This document explains how to use retry mechanism in TestNG in a simple, interview‑friendly, and practical way.

You will learn:

  • Retry at Test Method Level
  • Retry at Global Level (All Tests)
  • When and why to use each approach

docs.title: 🧠 What is Retry Mechanism?
docs.text:
Retry mechanism allows failed test cases to run again automatically before being marked as FAILED.

Common use cases:

  • Flaky Selenium tests
  • Temporary network / API issues
  • Unstable test environments

docs.title: 🧩 Core Component – RetryAnalyzer
docs.text:
This class contains the retry logic. It is mandatory for both approaches.

import org.testng.IRetryAnalyzer;
import org.testng.ITestResult;

public class RetryAnalyzer implements IRetryAnalyzer {

    private int retryCount = 0;
    private static final int MAX_RETRY = 2; // retry 2 times

    @Override
    public boolean retry(ITestResult result) {
        if (retryCount < MAX_RETRY) {
            retryCount++;
            System.out.println("Retrying test: " + result.getName() +
                    " | Retry count: " + retryCount);
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

📌 Total runs = 1 initial + 2 retries = 3 executions

docs.title: ✅ Approach 1: Retry at Test Method Level
📌 When to Use
docs.text:
• Only few tests are flaky
  • You want full control per test
  • Small test suite

docs.title: 🔹 How It Works
docs.text: RetryAnalyzer is attached directly to the test method using @Test annotation.

docs.title: 🔹 Snippet Code
docs.text:
import org.testng.Assert;
import org.testng.annotations.Test;

public class LoginTest {

    @Test(retryAnalyzer = RetryAnalyzer.class)
    public void loginTest() {
        System.out.println("Executing loginTest");
        Assert.assertTrue(false); // force failure
    }
}

docs.title: 🔄 Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. Test runs
  2. Test fails ❌
  3. RetryAnalyzer.retry() is called
  4. Test retries until MAX_RETRY is reached

docs.title: ✅ Pros
docs.text:
• Very simple
  • Easy to understand

docs.title: ❌ Cons
docs.text:
• Must add retry to every test method
  • Not scalable for large frameworks

docs.title: 🌍 Approach 2: Retry at Global Level (All Tests)
📌 When to Use
docs.text:
• Large automation framework
  • Many tests
  • Want centralized retry logic

👉 This is industry best practice

docs.title: 🔹 Step 1: Create RetryListener
docs.text:
This listener dynamically attaches RetryAnalyzer only when a test fails.

import org.testng.ITestContext;
import org.testng.ITestListener;
import org.testng.ITestResult;

public class RetryListener implements ITestListener {

    @Override
    public void onTestFailure(ITestResult result) {
        if (result.getMethod().getRetryAnalyzer() == null) {
            result.getMethod().setRetryAnalyzer(new RetryAnalyzer());
        }
    }

    @Override public void onTestStart(ITestResult result) {}
    @Override public void onTestSuccess(ITestResult result) {}
    @Override public void onTestSkipped(ITestResult result) {}
    @Override public void onTestFailedButWithinSuccessPercentage(ITestResult result) {}
    @Override public void onStart(ITestContext context) {}
    @Override public void onFinish(ITestContext context) {}
}

docs.title: 🔹 Step 2: Register Listener in testng.xml
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE suite SYSTEM "https://testng.org/testng-1.0.dtd">

<suite name="Retry Suite">

    <listeners>
        <listener class-name="RetryListener"/>
    </listeners>

    <test name="All Tests">
        <classes>
            <class name="LoginTest"/>
            <class name="PaymentTest"/>
        </classes>
    </test>

</suite>

docs.title: 🔹 Sample Test (No Retry Annotation Needed!)
docs.text:
import org.testng.Assert;
import org.testng.annotations.Test;

public class PaymentTest {

    @Test
    public void paymentTest() {
        System.out.println("Executing paymentTest");
        Assert.assertEquals(500, 200); // force failure
    }
}

📌 Retry happens automatically when test fails.

docs.title: 🔄 Execution Flow (Global Level)
docs.text:
1. Test executes
  2. Test fails ❌
  3. onTestFailure() listener is triggered
  4. RetryAnalyzer is attached dynamically
  5. Test is retried

docs.title: ✅ Pros
docs.text:
• No duplicate annotations
  • Clean test code
  • Scales well

docs.title: ❌ Cons
docs.text: • Slightly complex to understand initially

docs.title: 🆚 Test Level vs Global Level Comparison
docs.text: Feature Test Level Global Level Configuration Per test method One-time setup Scalability ❌ Poor ✅ Excellent Maintenance ❌ High ✅ Low Industry Usage ❌ Rare ✅ Very common

docs.title: ⚠️ Important Notes (Interview Points ⭐)
docs.text:
• Retry works only for FAILED tests
  • Retry does NOT work for PASSED tests
  • Retry count should be small (1–2)
  • Do NOT use retry to hide real bugs

docs.title: 🎯 Interview One‑Liner
docs.text:
"Using IRetryAnalyzer with ITestListener, we can apply retry logic globally so failed TestNG tests are automatically re‑executed without annotating each test method."

✅ End of Document

You can now download or reuse this .md file directly.

docs.title: 📘 TestNG Advanced Execution Guide (Complete with Full Code)
docs.text:
This guide covers:

✅ Dynamic Skip (SkipException) – full working code ✅ How TestNG internally uses ExecutorService (thread pool) ✅ How to exclude specific methods WITHOUT modifying XML structure ✅ Purpose + Use cases + Full runnable examples + Outputs

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Skip test dynamically at runtime based on condition.

docs.title: Full Working Code
docs.text:
package tests;

import org.testng.SkipException;
import org.testng.annotations.Test;

public class PaymentTest {

    @Test
    public void paymentGatewayTest() {

        boolean isGatewayDown = true;

        if (isGatewayDown) {
            throw new SkipException("Payment gateway is down → skipping test");
        }

        System.out.println("Payment processed");
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: SKIPPED: Payment gateway is down → skipping test

docs.title: 🔵 2️⃣ How threadCount Works Internally
docs.text:
TestNG internally uses Java ThreadPool similar to:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threadCount);

docs.title: Simplified Internal Flow
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

pool.submit(() -> testA());
pool.submit(() -> testB());
pool.submit(() -> testC());

pool.shutdown();

docs.title: TestNG Example
docs.text:
<suite parallel="methods" thread-count="2">

@Test
public void testA() {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getId());
}

@Test
public void testB() {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getId());
}

docs.title: Option A
docs.text: @Test(enabled = false)

docs.title: Option B (Groups)
docs.text:
@Test(groups = "slow")

XML:

<exclude name="slow"/>

docs.title: Option C (Method exclude)
docs.text:
<class name="tests.LoginTest">
    <methods>
        <exclude name="testPayment"/>
    </methods>
</class>

docs.title: Option D (Runtime)
docs.text:
throw new SkipException("Skip test");

docs.text:
@DataProvider(name="excelUsers")
public Object[][] excelUsers() throws Exception {

    FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("src/test/resources/users.xlsx");
    Workbook wb = new XSSFWorkbook(fis);
    Sheet sheet = wb.getSheetAt(0);

    int rows = sheet.getPhysicalNumberOfRows();

    Object[][] data = new Object[rows-1][4]; // 4 columns

    for(int i = 1; i < rows; i++) {

        Row row = sheet.getRow(i);

        data[i-1][0] = row.getCell(0).getStringCellValue();
        data[i-1][1] = row.getCell(1).getStringCellValue();
        data[i-1][2] = row.getCell(2).getStringCellValue();
        data[i-1][3] = row.getCell(3).getBooleanCellValue();
    }

    wb.close();
    return data;
}

docs.title: XML Sample file.
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE suite SYSTEM "https://testng.org/testng-1.0.dtd">

<suite name="EcommerceSuite" parallel="methods" thread-count="3">

    <!-- ================================================= -->
    <!-- TEST BLOCK 1 → Smoke Only -->
    <!-- ================================================= -->

    <test name="SmokeTests">

        <!-- Group include/exclude -->
        <groups>
            <run>
                <include name="smoke"/>
                <exclude name="slow"/>
            </run>
        </groups>

        <classes>

            <!-- Include entire class -->
            <class name="tests.LoginTest"/>

            <!-- Include class but exclude one method -->
            <class name="tests.PaymentTest">
                <methods>
                    <exclude name="paymentFailureTest"/>
                </methods>
            </class>

        </classes>

    </test>


    <!-- ================================================= -->
    <!-- TEST BLOCK 2 → Regression -->
    <!-- ================================================= -->

    <test name="RegressionTests">

        <groups>
            <run>
                <include name="regression"/>
            </run>
        </groups>

        <classes>

            <!-- Include only specific methods -->
            <class name="tests.OrderTest">
                <methods>
                    <include name="placeOrder"/>
                    <include name="cancelOrder"/>
                </methods>
            </class>

            <!-- Completely exclude class -->
            <class name="tests.LegacyTest">
                <methods>
                    <exclude name=".*"/>
                </methods>
            </class>

        </classes>

    </test>


    <!-- ================================================= -->
    <!-- TEST BLOCK 3 → Full Suite -->
    <!-- ================================================= -->

    <test name="FullSuite">

        <classes>

            <!-- Run everything -->
            <class name="tests.*"/>

        </classes>

    </test>

</suite>

public class Retry implements IRetryAnalyzer {
    int count = 0;

    public boolean retry(ITestResult result){
        if(count < 2){
            count++;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

@Test(retryAnalyzer = Retry.class)
